Perform an LP immediately and measure red cell count only
Start empirical IV antibiotics and aciclovir
Repeat the CT head in 24 hours
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.answer: Perform an LP at ≥12 hours from headache onset to look for xanthochromia
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: A normal early CT does not exclude SAH. LP is delayed to ≥12 hours to allow red cells to lyse and haemoglobin to be converted to bilirubin, producing xanthochromia detectable on spectrophotometry; this also distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap (which shows a falling RBC count tube 1→4 and no xanthochromia). Empirical antibiotics/aciclovir treat meningitis/encephalitis, not this thunderclap presentation.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.question: A traveller returns from West Africa with fever; the first malaria blood film is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Exclude malaria and investigate other causes
Start empirical antibiotics for typhoid
Repeat blood films — three over 48–72 hours before excluding malaria
Arrange a bone marrow aspirate
Reassure and discharge
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.answer: Repeat blood films — three over 48–72 hours before excluding malaria
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: A single negative film does not exclude malaria because parasitaemia is cyclical. Send three thick/thin films over 48–72 hours (± rapid antigen test) before excluding the diagnosis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.question: Wet-mount microscopy of vaginal discharge shows epithelial cells studded with coccobacilli giving stippled, obscured borders. What is the diagnosis?
options: Trichomonas vaginalis
Vulvovaginal candidiasis
Gonorrhoea
Chlamydia
Bacterial vaginosis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: These are clue cells — epithelial cells coated with coccobacilli (Gardnerella) with stippled borders — diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis (supported by pH >4.5 and a positive whiff test). Motile trophozoites would indicate Trichomonas.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 3-year-old with vomiting and watery diarrhoea has a stool multiplex PCR panel that returns positive for norovirus. Ten days later the child is clinically well and back to normal, but a repeat stool PCR (sent before school return) is still positive for norovirus. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Ongoing active norovirus infection requiring isolation until symptom-free for 14 days
A false-positive result from cross-reaction with rotavirus primers
Prolonged viral shedding of nucleic acid after clinical recovery
Secondary bacterial superinfection masking as norovirus
Chronic norovirus carriage causing an immunodeficiency syndrome
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Prolonged viral shedding of nucleic acid after clinical recovery
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: PCR detects nucleic acid, not viable virus. Norovirus (like SARS-CoV-2) is well recognised to shed detectable RNA for days to weeks after symptoms resolve. A persistent positive in a well child reflects shedding, not ongoing active disease, and does not by itself mandate continued exclusion. It is not a cross-reaction artefact or evidence of superinfection/immunodeficiency.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 68-year-old man is admitted with sepsis and a suspected respiratory source. A rapid respiratory PCR panel is positive for influenza A. Which single statement best reflects correct use and limitation of this result?
options: The panel result gives the antibiotic sensitivities needed to guide therapy
Culture is now unnecessary because PCR is more sensitive than culture in every situation
The positive PCR excludes any bacterial co-infection
Antivirals should be withheld until viral culture confirms viability
A positive influenza A result should prompt isolation/cohorting and consideration of oseltamivir, but gives no bacterial susceptibilities
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: A positive influenza A result should prompt isolation/cohorting and consideration of oseltamivir, but gives no bacterial susceptibilities
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: Rapid respiratory PCR guides infection control (isolation/cohorting) and antiviral decisions (oseltamivir for influenza). However, panels provide no antibiotic susceptibility data, and a viral positive does not exclude bacterial co-infection — culture is still needed where susceptibilities or bacteraemia matter. Waiting for viral culture would inappropriately delay antivirals.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: Compared with conventional bacterial culture, which of the following is the principal advantage that culture still holds over a multiplex PCR panel?
options: Faster turnaround time
Provision of antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Ability to detect non-culturable organisms
Higher analytical sensitivity for viral pathogens
Simultaneous detection of many targets from one sample
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: PCR panels are faster, highly sensitive, multi-target, and can detect fastidious/non-culturable organisms — all advantages over culture. The one thing culture still provides that PCR does not is antimicrobial susceptibility (sensitivity) testing on a viable isolate, which is why culture remains necessary when guiding targeted therapy.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 22-year-old man attends the sexual health clinic worried about urethral discharge after unprotected sex. Which sample is the preferred specimen for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT?
options: Midstream urine
Vulvovaginal swab
Blood for serology
First-catch (first-void) urine
Rectal swab only
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: In men the first-catch urine is the preferred NAAT sample as the first fraction carries the highest organism load; a midstream sample is used for urinary tract infection, not STI NAAT. Vulvovaginal swab is the sample of choice in women. Serology has no role in acute chlamydia/gonorrhoea diagnosis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 25-year-old woman has a positive gonorrhoea NAAT from a vulvovaginal swab. What is the most important additional microbiological step before starting antibiotics?
options: Take a culture (charcoal swab) for antimicrobial sensitivities
Repeat the NAAT to confirm
Send blood cultures
Start empirical doxycycline immediately
Request gonococcal serology
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Take a culture (charcoal swab) for antimicrobial sensitivities
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: NAAT confirms the diagnosis but provides no antibiotic sensitivities. Because of rising gonococcal resistance, a culture on a charcoal swab must be taken before treatment to allow sensitivity testing and guide/confirm therapy (IM ceftriaxone). Repeating the NAAT and serology do not give sensitivities.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 20-year-old asymptomatic woman requests STI screening. Regarding chlamydia, which statement is most accurate?
options: Symptoms are almost always present in women, so asymptomatic testing is unnecessary
Culture is the gold-standard first-line diagnostic test
She falls within the National Chlamydia Screening Programme age group (under-25s) and should be offered a vulvovaginal swab NAAT
Diagnosis should be confirmed by serology
First-line treatment is IM ceftriaxone
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: She falls within the National Chlamydia Screening Programme age group (under-25s) and should be offered a vulvovaginal swab NAAT
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: Chlamydia is frequently asymptomatic, especially in women, which is why the National Chlamydia Screening Programme targets sexually active under-25s using NAAT (self-taken vulvovaginal swab). NAAT — not culture or serology — is gold-standard/first-line, and chlamydia is treated with doxycycline; IM ceftriaxone is for gonorrhoea.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 4-year-old with known atopic eczema presents with a 2-day history of fever and a rapidly spreading rash of clustered, monomorphic, punched-out erosions over the face and flexures. He is miserable and off his feeds. Which is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Take a viral PCR swab and await the result before starting any antiviral therapy
Apply a potent topical corticosteroid to settle the eczema flare
Prescribe oral flucloxacillin alone and review in 48 hours
Reassure and advise emollients, as this is a routine eczema exacerbation
Start empirical aciclovir immediately and take a viral PCR swab from a deroofed vesicle
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Start empirical aciclovir immediately and take a viral PCR swab from a deroofed vesicle
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: This is eczema herpeticum, a dermatological emergency due to disseminated HSV. Aciclovir must be started empirically without waiting for the PCR result; the swab confirms the diagnosis. Watch for bacterial superinfection. Topical steroids alone or antibiotics alone are inadequate, and delaying treatment for the result is dangerous.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A GP wants to confirm and type the causative virus in a patient with a fresh crop of painful vesicles. Which sample and technique gives the highest diagnostic yield?
options: Swabbing a dry, crusted lesion for viral PCR
Deroofing a fresh vesicle and swabbing its base/fluid for viral PCR
A Tzanck smear from the vesicle roof
Serum antibody titres for HSV and VZV
Skin biopsy sent for routine histology
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Deroofing a fresh vesicle and swabbing its base/fluid for viral PCR
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: PCR of a swab from the base of a fresh, deroofed vesicle is the test of choice — rapid, highly sensitive/specific, and it types HSV vs VZV. Crusted lesions give false negatives. The Tzanck smear is outdated and cannot reliably distinguish HSV from VZV; serology and histology are not the confirmatory tests here.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 68-year-old presents with a 3-day fever, progressive confusion, and a witnessed seizure. MRI suggests temporal lobe involvement. Regarding CSF HSV PCR, which statement is correct?
options: IV aciclovir should be withheld until the CSF HSV PCR result returns
A negative Tzanck smear reliably excludes HSV encephalitis
CSF HSV PCR is unhelpful and lumbar puncture should be avoided entirely
Empirical IV aciclovir should be started immediately, without waiting for the PCR
Oral aciclovir is sufficient once the PCR confirms HSV
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Empirical IV aciclovir should be started immediately, without waiting for the PCR
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: HSV encephalitis is a life-threatening emergency. CSF HSV PCR is the confirmatory investigation, but empirical IV aciclovir must be started immediately as delay increases mortality and morbidity. The test does not replace clinical urgency, a Tzanck smear plays no role, and oral therapy is inadequate for encephalitis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A 4-year-old is brought in with fever, drowsiness and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. The GP gave IM benzylpenicillin 90 minutes ago. In hospital he receives IV ceftriaxone and is resuscitated. Blood cultures and CSF culture are subsequently reported as no growth. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the causative organism?
options: EDTA blood and CSF meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR
Repeat blood cultures off antibiotics
CSF Gram stain only
Serum procalcitonin
Throat swab culture
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: EDTA blood and CSF meningococcal/pneumococcal PCR
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: Pre-hospital and hospital antibiotics rapidly sterilise cultures, producing culture-negative disease. PCR detects bacterial DNA and remains positive after antibiotics, so it is the best test to confirm the organism retrospectively. Repeating cultures off antibiotics is unsafe and low-yield; Gram stain is often negative post-antibiotics; procalcitonin and throat swab do not confirm the pathogen.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A CSF meningococcal PCR returns positive with serogroup B in a confirmed case of meningococcal sepsis. Which statement about this result is correct?
options: It provides antibiotic sensitivities to guide definitive therapy
A positive PCR means culture must have also been positive
It should prompt notification to public health and contact prophylaxis
It excludes pneumococcal co-infection definitively
It replaces the need to give antibiotics
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: It should prompt notification to public health and contact prophylaxis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: Meningococcal disease is notifiable; a positive PCR with serogroup drives public-health action and contact prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin), and informs vaccination. PCR gives no sensitivities (culture needed for that), can be positive when culture is negative, does not exclude other pathogens, and antibiotics must always be given at first suspicion.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: Which single feature best explains why blood PCR is preferred over blood culture for confirming Neisseria meningitidis in UK practice?
options: PCR is cheaper than culture
PCR provides full antibiotic susceptibility data
PCR can be performed at the bedside in minutes
PCR requires no laboratory processing
PCR remains positive after antibiotics have been administered
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: PCR remains positive after antibiotics have been administered
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: Because antibiotics are given immediately (never delayed for LP), cultures are frequently sterile. PCR detects DNA and stays positive post-antibiotics, so it confirms the organism when culture cannot. PCR does not give susceptibilities, is not a bedside test, and still requires lab processing; cost is not the reason.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.question: A patient on antiretroviral therapy has a rising HIV RNA viral load after months of being undetectable. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A cure of the infection
Treatment failure from resistance or non-adherence
Laboratory contamination
Normal immune reconstitution
That the assay is qualitative only
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.answer: Treatment failure from resistance or non-adherence
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Molecular.explanation: The viral load is a quantitative marker trended over time: undetectable indicates good response (and untransmissibility), while a rising load signals treatment failure — resistance or, commonly, poor adherence — and prompts review.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 34-year-old man with 6 weeks of cough, weight loss and night sweats has a chest X-ray showing a right upper-lobe cavity. Three sputum samples are sent. The AFB smear (Ziehl-Neelsen) is reported as NEGATIVE. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the patient that pulmonary TB is excluded and discharge
Perform a Mantoux test to confirm active tuberculosis
Continue full investigation for active TB (culture and NAAT) and manage as suspected infectious TB with isolation
Repeat the chest X-ray in 6 weeks before any further action
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia only
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Continue full investigation for active TB (culture and NAAT) and manage as suspected infectious TB with isolation
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: AFB smear has low sensitivity (needs ~10,000 bacilli/mL), so a negative smear does NOT exclude TB. With a classic history and a cavitating upper-lobe lesion, TB remains highly likely: send culture (gold standard) and NAAT/GeneXpert, isolate, and treat as suspected infectious TB. Mantoux tests latent infection, not active disease, and cannot confirm active TB.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A GeneXpert MTB/RIF test on a sputum sample returns positive for M. tuberculosis and additionally detects rifampicin resistance. What is the single most important implication of the rifampicin-resistance result?
options: It confirms the patient has latent rather than active TB
It indicates the smear must have been falsely positive
It means the culture will be negative
It rules out the need for drug-susceptibility testing on culture
It is a surrogate marker for multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and should prompt specialist regimen adjustment and infection control
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: It is a surrogate marker for multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and should prompt specialist regimen adjustment and infection control
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: GeneXpert detects rpoB mutations conferring rifampicin resistance, which is used as a surrogate marker for MDR-TB (resistance to at least rifampicin and isoniazid). This rapid flag guides early escalation to a specialist regimen and reinforces infection-control measures. Full culture-based drug-susceptibility testing is still performed to define the complete resistance profile.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A medical student is asked which single test is the gold standard for diagnosing active pulmonary tuberculosis because it is the most sensitive and uniquely provides drug-susceptibility information. Which is it?
options: Ziehl-Neelsen sputum smear microscopy
Löwenstein-Jensen / MGIT culture
Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)
Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux)
Chest X-ray
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Culture (solid LJ or liquid MGIT) is the gold standard: it is the most sensitive test, confirms the species, and crucially provides drug-susceptibility testing to guide therapy. Its limitation is that it is slow (weeks). Smear is fast but insensitive and non-specific; IGRA and Mantoux test latent infection/immune sensitisation, not active disease; chest X-ray is supportive but non-diagnostic.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 68-year-old man is admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia after returning from a hotel spa holiday. He is confused, has profuse diarrhoea, sodium 126 mmol/L and ALT 180 U/L. His Legionella urinary antigen test is negative. What is the single most appropriate interpretation and action?
options: A negative test reliably excludes Legionella, so continue amoxicillin alone
Repeat the pneumococcal antigen instead, as Legionella is now ruled out
Stop all antibiotics as no pathogen has been confirmed
The test only detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so Legionella is not excluded — cover with a macrolide or quinolone
Switch to a beta-lactam alone as it adequately covers Legionella
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: The test only detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so Legionella is not excluded — cover with a macrolide or quinolone
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: The Legionella urinary antigen detects serogroup 1 ONLY, so a negative result does not exclude infection with other serogroups/species. With a highly suggestive picture (severe CAP, hyponatraemia, deranged LFTs, diarrhoea, confusion, spa exposure) empirical atypical cover with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone is essential — beta-lactams alone do not cover Legionella. Legionnaires' is also notifiable.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A patient with moderate CAP was started on antibiotics 48 hours ago before samples were taken; blood and sputum cultures are now negative. Which investigation is most likely to still identify a causative organism?
options: Urinary antigen tests for pneumococcus and Legionella
Repeat blood cultures
Sputum Gram stain and culture
Serum procalcitonin
Full blood count and CRP
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Urinary antigen tests for pneumococcus and Legionella
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: The defining advantage of urinary antigen tests is that they remain positive after antibiotics have been started, whereas cultures are rapidly rendered negative. Procalcitonin and CRP are non-specific inflammatory markers and do not identify an organism.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: Which statement about pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests is correct?
options: They provide antibiotic sensitivity results to guide therapy
The pneumococcal test is most reliable in young children
They can remain positive after antibiotics but provide no antibiotic sensitivities
A negative pneumococcal antigen excludes all bacterial pneumonia
Legionella antigen detects all Legionella species and serogroups
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: They can remain positive after antibiotics but provide no antibiotic sensitivities
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Both tests stay positive after antibiotic initiation, aiding diagnosis when cultures fail — but they yield no sensitivities and detect only specific targets (pneumococcal C-polysaccharide; Legionella serogroup 1). The pneumococcal test is unreliable in children due to nasopharyngeal carriage, and a negative result never excludes infection.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 22-year-old, previously well student presents with 10 days of gradually worsening dry cough, malaise and low-grade fever. Chest X-ray shows patchy bilateral consolidation that appears more extensive than his relatively mild clinical state. Bloods show a mild anaemia with jaundice, and the FBC analyser flags red-cell clumping. Which single investigation would best confirm the underlying respiratory pathogen?
options: Cold agglutinin titre
Sputum Gram stain and culture
Blood film for red-cell agglutination
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
Mycoplasma PCR of a respiratory sample
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Mycoplasma PCR of a respiratory sample
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: The picture is atypical pneumonia with a cold AIHA, strongly suggesting Mycoplasma. Cold agglutinins and a blood film are non-specific supportive clues only and can be positive in EBV/lymphoproliferative disease. Gram stain/culture is unreliable as Mycoplasma has no cell wall and is not easily cultured. Confirmation is by Mycoplasma serology (paired titres) or PCR, of which PCR is the single best rapid confirmatory test here.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 19-year-old with confirmed Mycoplasma pneumoniae was started on amoxicillin by a colleague but has failed to improve after 3 days. What is the correct explanation and next step?
options: The dose is too low; increase the amoxicillin dose
Mycoplasma has no cell wall so beta-lactams fail; switch to clarithromycin
She has developed a resistant strain; add a cephalosporin
The diagnosis is wrong; stop all antibiotics
She needs IV benzylpenicillin instead of oral amoxicillin
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Mycoplasma has no cell wall so beta-lactams fail; switch to clarithromycin
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall, so beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) that target cell-wall synthesis are intrinsically ineffective regardless of dose or route. Appropriate treatment is a macrolide such as clarithromycin, or a tetracycline such as doxycycline.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A patient with atypical pneumonia is found to have a positive cold agglutinin test. Which statement is most accurate regarding this finding?
options: It is specific for Mycoplasma pneumoniae and confirms the diagnosis
It excludes EBV as a cause of the illness
It indicates warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
It is a non-specific supportive clue that can also occur in EBV and lymphoproliferative disease
It rules out any need for antibiotic treatment
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: It is a non-specific supportive clue that can also occur in EBV and lymphoproliferative disease
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Cold agglutinins are a classic but non-specific and largely historical clue to Mycoplasma. They are IgM antibodies causing a cold (not warm) AIHA and can also be positive in EBV, other infections and lymphoproliferative disease, so they neither confirm Mycoplasma nor exclude other causes. Confirmation requires serology or PCR.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 34-year-old man with epigastric pain is being investigated for H. pylori. He has been taking omeprazole 20 mg daily for the last 3 weeks. His GP requests a urea breath test. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop the omeprazole for at least 2 weeks before the breath test
Proceed with the breath test today as PPIs do not affect the result
Perform serology instead as it is unaffected by PPIs
Start eradication therapy empirically without any test
Switch to an H2-receptor antagonist and test the same day
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Stop the omeprazole for at least 2 weeks before the breath test
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: PPIs suppress H. pylori and cause false-negative urea breath, stool antigen and CLO tests. PPIs should be stopped for at least 2 weeks (and antibiotics/bismuth for at least 4 weeks) before testing. Serology is not recommended as it cannot distinguish current from past infection.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 41-year-old woman completed 7 days of triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) for a duodenal ulcer 6 weeks ago. Her GP wants to confirm eradication. Which is the most appropriate test of cure?
options: Serology for H. pylori IgG antibodies
Repeat OGD with CLO test as first choice
Urea breath test
Full blood count and CRP
Fasting gastrin level
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: The urea breath test (or stool antigen test) is the preferred non-invasive test of cure, performed at least 4–8 weeks after completing eradication therapy. Serology is inappropriate because antibodies remain positive after successful eradication. Endoscopy is invasive and not required as first-line test of cure here.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 62-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of new dyspepsia, 5 kg unintentional weight loss and one episode of melaena. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Non-invasive H. pylori stool antigen test and treat if positive
Empirical triple eradication therapy
Trial of over-the-counter antacids and review in 3 months
Serology for H. pylori and PPI trial
Urgent (2-week-wait) upper GI endoscopy
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Alarm features — age ≥55 with new persistent dyspepsia, weight loss and GI bleeding (melaena) — mandate an urgent 2-week-wait upper GI endoscopy to exclude malignancy, rather than a test-and-treat strategy. H. pylori testing is reserved for uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A blood culture grows E. coli. The laboratory performs a gradient strip (E-test) with meropenem and reads the point where the elliptical zone of inhibition meets the strip. What does this reading represent?
options: The minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC)
The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)
The zone of inhibition diameter in mm
The serum bactericidal titre
The breakpoint set by EUCAST
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: An E-test / gradient strip carries a continuous antibiotic gradient; the value where the elliptical growth-inhibition zone intersects the strip is the direct MIC — the lowest concentration inhibiting visible growth. The MBC (kills 99.9%) is a separate measurement, disc diffusion gives a zone diameter rather than a numeric MIC, and the breakpoint is the reference value the MIC is compared against, not the reading itself.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A patient with an S. aureus vertebral osteomyelitis is treated with an antibiotic reported as "Susceptible" on the sensitivity panel but fails to improve after several days. Which single factor best explains treatment failure despite in-vitro susceptibility?
options: The EUCAST breakpoint was set too low
The organism must have been mis-identified by the laboratory
Susceptibility testing is unreliable for Gram-positive organisms
Poor antibiotic penetration into bone at the site of infection
The MIC was higher than the MBC for this isolate
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: Poor antibiotic penetration into bone at the site of infection
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: In-vitro susceptibility does not guarantee clinical cure. Bone (like CNS, prostate and biofilm) is a poorly penetrated site, so an agent labelled "S" may not reach adequate concentrations there. Interpretation must always account for the site of infection, penetration and the need for source control — not just the S/I/R label.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A urine sample sent for PCR returns positive for a carbapenemase gene, but no organism has been cultured. The FY1 asks which antibiotics the bug is sensitive to. What is the most accurate response?
options: No sensitivities are available — susceptibility testing requires a viable cultured isolate
Report the isolate as pan-sensitive since PCR was positive
Start empirical carbapenem therapy as the gene predicts susceptibility
The PCR result gives a full EUCAST S/I/R panel automatically
Sensitivities can be inferred directly from the zone of inhibition on the PCR plate
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.answer: No sensitivities are available — susceptibility testing requires a viable cultured isolate
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: Molecular tests identify organisms or specific resistance genes but cannot produce a susceptibility panel — that needs a viable isolate exposed to antibiotics in culture. A carbapenemase gene actually flags likely carbapenem RESISTANCE, warranting escalation to microbiology/ID rather than empirical carbapenem use. Only culture yields sensitivities.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A 24-year-old BCG-vaccinated healthcare worker needs screening after a TB contact. Which test best distinguishes latent TB infection from a BCG reaction?
options: Mantoux (tuberculin skin test)
Sputum smear for AFB
Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)
Chest X-ray
GeneXpert MTB/RIF
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: IGRA uses M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6/CFP-10) not present in BCG, so it is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination — unlike Mantoux, which can be falsely positive after BCG. Smear/GeneXpert/CXR test for active disease, not latent infection.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.question: A patient with a lymphocytic CSF, high protein and low glucose has a raised CSF adenosine deaminase (ADA). Which diagnosis does this pattern most support?
options: Bacterial meningitis
Viral meningitis
Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Guillain-Barre syndrome
Tuberculous meningitis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__TB, Atypic.explanation: A lymphocytic CSF with high protein, low glucose and raised ADA is characteristic of tuberculous meningitis. Bacterial meningitis is neutrophilic; viral meningitis has normal glucose; ADA is a useful pointer to TB in CSF and serosal fluids.
